steps.name: One object, three viewpoints
steps.narration: We are looking at a solid made from a cube. Plans and elevations are flat drawings of the very same object, seen from different directions.
steps.prompt: Why would a builder need more than one view?

steps.name: Look straight down — the top plan
steps.narration: Look straight down on the cube. Its top plan is one square. A plan tells us where the solid covers the floor, but does not show its height.
steps.prompt: What shape do you see in the top plan?

steps.name: Face the solid — the front elevation
steps.narration: Look horizontally from the front. The front elevation shows width and height, not how far back the cube goes.
steps.prompt: Which dimension disappears from the front elevation?

steps.name: Turn right — the side elevation
steps.narration: Now look from the right-hand side. The right-side elevation shows depth and height. The front-to-back direction runs left to right in this view.
steps.prompt: Does the right-side view show width or depth?

steps.name: Four cubes — one large top plan
steps.narration: A two by two platform uses four cubes. From above, we see four squares, but from the front we see only two. The same solid has different views.
steps.prompt: How many squares appear from above?

steps.name: Height changes elevations
steps.narration: This two-high stack still covers one square in its plan. Both elevations rise to two squares high. Taller solids do not necessarily have bigger plans.
steps.prompt: How has the top plan changed?

steps.name: A corner shape makes different outlines
steps.narration: This corner has two cubes in one column, and one cube in each of two neighbouring columns. Read the plan first, then find the highest stack in every front and side line.

steps.name: Each elevation shows the maximum height

steps.prompt: Why does the side view show just one tall column?

data.narration: Count the solid unit cubes, including hidden cubes inside the stack. Volume measures the space filled, not the number of visible faces or surface squares.

steps.name: A cube is one unit of volume
steps.narration: This is a unit cube. It takes up one cubic unit of space. A cube with edges one centimetre long has a volume of one cubic centimetre.
steps.prompt: What does one unit cube measure?

steps.name: Build a horizontal row
steps.narration: A straight row of four unit cubes has a volume of four cubic units. We can count each one.
steps.prompt: How many cubes are in the row?

steps.name: Make a base layer
steps.narration: Now arrange three cubes along the length and two across the width. Each complete layer has six cubes, because three times two equals six.
steps.prompt: Why are there six cubes in this layer?

steps.name: One layer is an area
steps.narration: The first layer is three by two, so it has six cubes. That is the base area measured in square units. We will need the height to calculate volume.
steps.prompt: Is the base area the volume yet?

steps.name: Stack a second layer
steps.narration: Add a second identical layer above the first. Now six plus six makes twelve unit cubes. That is two layers of six.
steps.prompt: What does the second layer add?

steps.name: Build three layers
steps.narration: The third layer adds another six. Three layers of six cubes give eighteen cubic units altogether.
steps.prompt: Count the layers to check eighteen.

steps.name: Link stacking to a formula
steps.narration: For a cuboid, multiply its length by its width by its height. Three times two times three equals eighteen cubic units.
steps.prompt: Which numbers count the cubes in a layer and the number of layers?

steps.name: A two-by-two-by-two cube
steps.narration: This cube has two rows and two columns in every layer. There are four cubes per layer and two layers, making eight unit cubes.
steps.prompt: How many cubes are hidden by the visible faces?

steps.name: Not every solid has equal layers
steps.narration: This stepped solid has three cubes on the bottom, two on the second layer, and one on the third. Add three, two and one to find six cubic units. The cuboid formula is not suitable for this stepped shape.
steps.prompt: Why is length times width times height misleading here?

data.name: The universal rule
data.narration: Every prism follows the same rule: volume equals cross-sectional area multiplied by perpendicular length.
data.prompt: Which measurement must you calculate first?

steps.name: Meet a prism
steps.narration: This 3D solid is a prism: the same cross-section runs from one end to the other.
steps.prompt: Which face keeps the same shape along the entire prism?

steps.name: Spot the repeated cross-section
steps.narration: Move the golden slicing plane. Every slice through the prism is the same rectangle.
steps.prompt: Does the shape or size of the cross-section change?

steps.name: Find the base area
steps.narration: The rectangular cross-section measures three by two. Its area is six square units.
steps.prompt: Why are square units used for a cross-section?

steps.name: Stretch along the length
steps.narration: The rectangular area stays six square units. Making the prism longer adds more identical layers.
steps.prompt: Which measurement changed: area or length?

steps.name: Multiply area by length
steps.narration: There are five unit lengths, each with an area of six. Six times five equals thirty cubic units.
steps.prompt: Explain why the final unit must be cubed.

steps.name: Meet a triangular prism
steps.narration: This time the constant cross-section is a right triangle with base four and perpendicular height three.
steps.prompt: What is the area formula for a triangle?

steps.name: Calculate its triangular area
steps.narration: Half times four times three is six square units. That is the cross-sectional area.
steps.prompt: Why is there a one-half in the triangle area formula?

steps.name: Find triangular-prism volume
steps.narration: Six square units repeated for four units of length gives twenty-four cubic units.
steps.prompt: What is six multiplied by four?

steps.name: A trapezium cross-section
steps.narration: The parallel sides are four and two. Half their sum, multiplied by the perpendicular height three, is nine square units.
steps.prompt: Which two sides of this trapezium are parallel?

steps.name: Composite L-shaped cross-section
steps.narration: A four by three rectangle has area twelve. Remove a two by two corner of area four: eight square units remain.
steps.prompt: How does removing a corner affect the total volume?

STEPS.q: Does the size of this cube section change?

STEPS.m: A triangular prism has a triangle at every horizontal height. The same triangle repeats along the whole length of the prism.

steps.name: Outside, not inside
steps.narration: Surface area is the amount of square units covering the OUTSIDE of a solid. There are six faces on a cuboid.
steps.prompt: Do we count the space inside? No: that is volume.

steps.name: Find the hidden faces
steps.narration: Some faces are hidden from this angle, but still contribute to the total surface area.
steps.prompt: How many of the six rectangles must be counted?

steps.name: Open along the hinges
steps.narration: Each face rotates around a shared edge. The sides never stretch, and the fold lines stay connected.
steps.prompt: Are the faces still the same sizes?

steps.name: Lay the net flat
steps.narration: This flat net has all six faces. A net is the surface of the solid laid out without overlaps.
steps.prompt: Can you identify the top and bottom rectangles?

steps.name: Count the top and bottom
steps.narration: The base and top are each four by three, so each has area twelve square units. Their combined area is twenty-four.
steps.prompt: Why do we count both twelve-unit faces?

steps.name: Add the front and back
steps.narration: The front and back measure four by two, giving eight each. Our running subtotal is forty square units.
steps.prompt: How many square units did this pair add?

steps.name: Add both end faces
steps.narration: Each end measures three by two, giving six each. Twelve more produces a total of fifty-two square units.
steps.prompt: Is fifty-two in square units or cubic units?

steps.name: A cube has equal squares
steps.narration: All six faces on a cube are equal squares. Three times three is nine, and six times nine is fifty-four.
steps.prompt: Why can we multiply one face area by six?

steps.name: A prism has two triangles

steps.prompt: Do we include the triangular ends?

steps.name: Area of triangular ends
steps.narration: The two equilateral triangular ends must both be counted. Their area can use one half base times perpendicular height.
steps.prompt: Why does the sloping edge not give the triangle height?

steps.name: Pyramid faces
steps.narration: A square pyramid has one square base and four triangular faces. Its face height is the slant height.
steps.prompt: Why is the vertical height not the height of each sloping face?

steps.name: Add all four triangles
steps.narration: The base covers sixteen squares. Each triangle covers six. Four triangles add twenty-four, so total area is forty square units.

steps.narration: A square face becomes two times wider and two times taller. Two times two makes four. Its AREA grows by four.

steps.narration: The solid grows in length, width AND height. Two times two times two makes eight times the volume.

steps.narration: The enlarged cube measures four by four by four. It contains sixty-four cubic units, eight times the original.
steps.prompt: Does doubling a solid double its volume?

steps.name: Cuboid · edge factor
